{{Short description|Mathematical conjecture}}
In [[model theory]], a branch of [[mathematical logic]], '''Chang's conjecture''', attributed to [[Chen Chung Chang]] by {{harvtxt|Vaught|1963|p=309}}, states that every model of type (ω<sub>2</sub>,ω<sub>1</sub>) for a [[countable]] [[first-order language|language]] has an [[elementary submodel]] of type (ω<sub>1</sub>,ω). A model is of type (''α'',''β'') if it is of cardinality ''α'' and a unary relation is represented by a subset of cardinality ''β''. The usual notation is <math>(\omega_2,\omega_1)\twoheadrightarrow(\omega_1,\omega)</math>.

The [[axiom of constructibility]] implies that Chang's conjecture fails. [[Jack Silver|Silver]] proved the consistency of Chang's conjecture from the consistency of an ω<sub>1</sub>-[[Erdős cardinal]]. Hans-Dieter Donder showed a weak version of the reverse implication: if Chang's conjecture is not only consistent but actually holds, then ω<sub>2</sub> is ω<sub>1</sub>-Erdős in [[core model|K]].

More generally, Chang's conjecture for two pairs (''α'',''β''), (''γ'',''δ'') of cardinals is the claim
that every model of type (''α'',''β'') for a countable language has an elementary submodel of type (''γ'',''δ''). 
The consistency of <math>(\omega_3,\omega_2)\twoheadrightarrow(\omega_2,\omega_1)</math> was shown by [[Richard Laver|Laver]] from the consistency of a [[huge cardinal]].
